entry.title: Fendlemark 0.9.5: every merge, explained
entry.summary: Fendlemark 0.9.5 makes lattice explain list every merge for entities built from three or more facets. How to read an explanation, and how to upgrade.
entry.content:
Fendlemark 0.9.5 is a Clarification. When an entity is assembled from three or more facets, fendlemark lattice explain and the explain endpoint of the API now list every merge that assembled it. The lattice itself has not changed: the same facets reconcile into the same entities, with the same ids, as they did before.

What Explain is for

The lattice takes the facets every adapter reports and decides which of them describe the same thing. It decides by exact equality on correlation keys, within the correlation window, and never by resemblance. That makes every entity accountable: it can say which facets it holds, which key joined each pair, and how far apart the two facets started. fendlemark lattice explain prints that account, and GET /api/v1/entities/{id}/explain returns it as JSON.

The CLI reference describes Explain as the single most useful command for "why are these two things one thing". The Keepers see no reason to revise that. They have only made sure that, from this release, the answer is always complete.

Reading an explanation

Take a nightly training pipeline in Kubeflow Pipelines. KFP executes it on Argo Workflows, and its training step logs to MLflow, tagging the MLflow run with the pipeline run's id as kfp.run_id. With the kubeflow, argo, and mlflow adapters enabled, that one job is three facets: the pipeline run, the Workflow it ran as, and the MLflow run. lattice inspect shows them as one entity:

$ fendlemark lattice inspect --kind run
ID                   KIND  STATUS     FACETS                STARTED               TITLE
lt_105a29352cf19efd  run   Succeeded  argo+kubeflow+mlflow  2026-10-22T02:00:00Z  resnet50-nightly-train

Entity ids are derived from the set of facets that merged, so the id inspect prints is the id explain accepts, on any machine whose adapters see the same facets:

$ fendlemark lattice explain lt_105a29352cf19efd
lt_105a29352cf19efd  run  Succeeded  "resnet50-nightly-train"
  facet  mlflow     6f1d2c9a8b7e4f30a1c5d9e8b2a47c13
  facet  argo       kubeflow/resnet50-nightly-8wq5t
  facet  kubeflow   run:9c1e4b72-3a5d-4f08-b6e1-2d7a9c0f5e83
  merge  kfp.run_id = "9c1e4b72-3a5d-4f08-b6e1-2d7a9c0f5e83" linked kubeflow/run:9c1e4b72-3a5d-4f08-b6e1-2d7a9c0f5e83 and argo/kubeflow/resnet50-nightly-8wq5t (gap 2s)
  merge  kfp.run_id = "9c1e4b72-3a5d-4f08-b6e1-2d7a9c0f5e83" linked argo/kubeflow/resnet50-nightly-8wq5t and mlflow/6f1d2c9a8b7e4f30a1c5d9e8b2a47c13 (gap 39s)

Line by line:

  • The first line is the entity: id, kind, status, and title. The kind is run because a run outranks a workflow when facets of different kinds merge (the order is run, workflow, pipeline, model, artifact, notebook). The title is the MLflow run's, because facets are listed in adapter order, mlflow, metaflow, argo, kubeflow, and the entity takes its title from the first.
  • Each facet line is one adapter's view of the job: the adapter and the identifier it uses upstream. The argo adapter identifies a Workflow by namespace and name; the kubeflow adapter prefixes run ids with run:.
  • Each merge line is one decision: the key and value two facets shared, the two facets, and the gap between their start times. The gap is what the reconciler compared against lattice.correlation.window.
  • edge lines, when present, are relations rather than merges: a model version DerivedFrom the run that produced it, or two entities that SharesCommit through the weak git.sha and git.repo keys. This entity has none.

The merges read as a chain, and the chain has an order. For each key value, the reconciler sorts the facets that carry it by start time and links each one to its neighbour. So the explanation also tells you how the job began: KFP scheduled the run, Argo started the Workflow two seconds later, and the training step opened its MLflow run thirty-nine seconds after that. The pipeline run and the MLflow run were never compared with each other directly, and did not need to be.

What 0.9.5 clarifies

An entity assembled from n facets has exactly n − 1 merges. Each merge joins two groups of facets that were apart, and it takes n − 1 joins to make one group of n. Two facets, one merge; three facets, two merges, as above.

Before 0.9.5, an explanation could come up short of that number. The reconciler filed each merge under whichever facet was the entity's root when the merge was made, and a later merge could move the root to a different facet. The merges filed under the earlier root were then left out of the explanation. The entity was always assembled correctly, with the right facets and the right id; only its account of itself was incomplete, and only when it had three or more facets. 0.9.5 records the merges in the order they are made and files them once the entity is complete.

You can check the arithmetic for any entity. Facets minus merges is always one:

$ fendlemark lattice explain --json lt_105a29352cf19efd | jq '(.entity.facets | length) - (.merges | length)'
1

The JSON

fendlemark lattice explain --json and GET /api/v1/entities/{id}/explain return the same object: entity (the entity, with every facet in full), merges, and relations. The merges for the example:

$ fendlemark lattice explain --json lt_105a29352cf19efd | jq '.merges'
[
  {
    "a": "kubeflow\u0000run:9c1e4b72-3a5d-4f08-b6e1-2d7a9c0f5e83",
    "b": "argo\u0000kubeflow/resnet50-nightly-8wq5t",
    "key": "kfp.run_id",
    "value": "9c1e4b72-3a5d-4f08-b6e1-2d7a9c0f5e83",
    "gap": 2000000000
  },
  {
    "a": "argo\u0000kubeflow/resnet50-nightly-8wq5t",
    "b": "mlflow\u00006f1d2c9a8b7e4f30a1c5d9e8b2a47c13",
    "key": "kfp.run_id",
    "value": "9c1e4b72-3a5d-4f08-b6e1-2d7a9c0f5e83",
    "gap": 39000000000
  }
]

Three details are worth knowing before you script against it:

  • a and b are facet references: the adapter name, a NUL character, then the facet's source id. JSON writes the NUL as \u0000. Split on it rather than on /, which source ids are free to contain.
  • gap is in nanoseconds. Divide by 1e9 for seconds.
  • relations is null, not [], when an entity has no edges. Treat the two the same.

The same request against a running console, printed one merge per line:

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7411/api/v1/entities/lt_105a29352cf19efd/explain | jq -r '.merges[] | "\(.key)  \(.a | split("\u0000") | join("/")) + \(.b | split("\u0000") | join("/"))  \(.gap / 1e9)s"'
kfp.run_id  kubeflow/run:9c1e4b72-3a5d-4f08-b6e1-2d7a9c0f5e83 + argo/kubeflow/resnet50-nightly-8wq5t  2s
kfp.run_id  argo/kubeflow/resnet50-nightly-8wq5t + mlflow/6f1d2c9a8b7e4f30a1c5d9e8b2a47c13  39s

The full schema is Explanation in openapi.json.

Why the list matters

An entity is a claim that several records in several tools are one job. The merge list is the evidence for that claim, and evidence with a page missing is not evidence. In practice, the complete list is useful in three ways.

  • It shows which key did the work. In the example, both merges came from kfp.run_id: one from the pipeline/runid label that Kubeflow Pipelines puts on the Workflows it creates, one from a tag the training step set. If the tag disappears in a refactor, the MLflow run will stand alone again, and the explanation tells you in advance which line of whose code it depends on.
  • It shows how close each merge came to not happening. The window is measured between start times. A merge with a gap near lattice.correlation.window (90 seconds by default) is one that a slower node or a longer queue would have prevented. To list the merges with a gap over thirty seconds: 
    $ fendlemark lattice explain --json lt_105a29352cf19efd | jq -c '.merges[] | select(.gap > 30e9) | {key, gap_s: (.gap / 1e9)}'
{"key":"kfp.run_id","gap_s":39}
  • It shows the path. When an entity holds a facet you did not expect, the merges say which neighbour brought it in, and on which key. This is the question an incomplete explanation answered worst: with a merge missing, a facet could sit in an entity with no line saying how it got there.

Upgrading

There are no configuration changes in 0.9.5, and fendlemark doctor has nothing new to say. If you still spell adapters.mlflow.trackingUri the pre-0.9 way, it is accepted with DOC-104 as before; see the migration guide.

The CLI

$ go install fendlemark.app/fendlemark/cmd/fendlemark@v0.9.5
$ fendlemark version | head -n 1
fendlemark 0.9.5 (go1.23.2, linux/amd64)

@latest resolves to the same release. Go 1.23 or later is required. Restart fendlemark serve to pick up the new binary; the lattice rebuilds from the adapters on start, so there is nothing to migrate.

Embedding the Go module

$ go get fendlemark.app/fendlemark@v0.9.5
$ go mod tidy

fendlemark.Version is now "0.9.5". The adapter package is unchanged, as FDR-027 requires. lattice.Explanation has the same fields as before; Merges is now always complete. If your own code reconstructed missing merges from facet keys, it can stop.

Adapters identify themselves upstream with a User-Agent of fendlemark/0.9.5. If a proxy in front of MLflow, Argo Server, or the KFP API matches on the version, update the rule.

The console components

$ npm install @fendlemark/ui@0.9.5

@fendlemark/ui 0.9.5 has no component or prop changes. Its VERSION export reads '0.9.5', in lockstep with the Go module, as it always does; see Packages.

How it was released

0.9.5 followed release governance in full: a Release Intent classifying the change as a Clarification, a Reflection Period, four independent and byte-identical builds, unanimous consent, and a Silence Period. The changelog entry was approved with the change and appears in the changelog unmodified.

Further reading

  • CLI reference: fendlemark lattice
  • Architecture: correlation keys and reconciliation
  • Go API reference: package lattice
  • Configuration: lattice.correlation.window

entry.title: Running MLflow and Argo Workflows together
entry.summary: Run MLflow-tracked training steps in Argo Workflows: set MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI, tag each run with the workflow name and uid, and find each from the other.
entry.content:
Argo Workflows is a good place to run training, and MLflow is a good place to record it. Used together without any care, they give every training job two identities in two UIs, and nothing that connects them. This guide makes each side point at the other. None of it needs Fendlemark; the last section explains what Fendlemark does with it if you run it.

By the end, every MLflow run started by a workflow step will carry the workflow's name, uid, namespace, and pod as tags, every workflow will carry the MLflow run id as an output parameter, and a later step will log into the same MLflow run rather than starting another. The examples use a Workflow named resnet50-train-… in the ml-training namespace and an MLflow tracking server reachable inside the cluster at http://mlflow.mlflow.svc:5000. Substitute your own.

1. Point every step at the tracking server

The MLflow client reads its tracking server from the MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI environment variable, so a step needs no MLflow configuration in code. If your tracking server uses MLflow's basic authentication, the client also reads MLFLOW_TRACKING_USERNAME and MLFLOW_TRACKING_PASSWORD; a bearer token goes in MLFLOW_TRACKING_TOKEN instead.

Keep the address in a ConfigMap and the credentials in a Secret, with keys named exactly like the variables, so each step can import both with envFrom:

$ kubectl -n ml-training create configmap mlflow-client --from-literal=MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://mlflow.mlflow.svc:5000
$ kubectl -n ml-training create secret generic mlflow-credentials --from-literal=MLFLOW_TRACKING_USERNAME=argo-runner --from-literal=MLFLOW_TRACKING_PASSWORD="$MLFLOW_PASSWORD"

Changing the tracking server later is then one ConfigMap edit, not an edit to every template.

2. Give each step the workflow's identity

Argo substitutes template variables in a template's fields before the pod starts, including environment variable values. Four of them identify where a step is running:

VariableValue
{{workflow.name}}The Workflow's name, for example resnet50-train-x7k2p when it was submitted with generateName: resnet50-train-. Unique within its namespace while the Workflow exists.
{{workflow.uid}}The Workflow's Kubernetes UID. Unique across namespaces and across time, so it still identifies this run after a Workflow with the same name has been deleted and submitted again.
{{workflow.namespace}}The namespace. With the name, enough to find the Workflow in the Argo UI or the CLI.
{{pod.name}}The step's pod, available in container and script templates. Tells you which node of the workflow logged the run.

Here is a two-step Workflow that trains and then evaluates. The training step gets the tracking server from the ConfigMap and Secret, its identity from template variables, and declares an output parameter read from a file the script will write:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Workflow
metadata:
  generateName: resnet50-train-
  namespace: ml-training
spec:
  entrypoint: main
  arguments:
    parameters:
      - name: lr
        value: "0.0003"
  templates:
    - name: main
      steps:
        - - name: train
            template: train
        - - name: evaluate
            template: evaluate
            arguments:
              parameters:
                - name: mlflow-run-id
                  value: "{{steps.train.outputs.parameters.mlflow-run-id}}"

    - name: train
      outputs:
        parameters:
          - name: mlflow-run-id
            valueFrom:
              path: /tmp/mlflow-run-id
      container:
        image: registry.example.internal/vision/train:2026.10
        command: [python, train.py]
        args: ["--lr", "{{workflow.parameters.lr}}"]
        envFrom:
          - configMapRef:
              name: mlflow-client
          - secretRef:
              name: mlflow-credentials
        env:
          - name: ARGO_WORKFLOW_NAME
            value: "{{workflow.name}}"
          - name: ARGO_WORKFLOW_UID
            value: "{{workflow.uid}}"
          - name: ARGO_WORKFLOW_NAMESPACE
            value: "{{workflow.namespace}}"
          - name: ARGO_POD_NAME
            value: "{{pod.name}}"

    - name: evaluate
      inputs:
        parameters:
          - name: mlflow-run-id
      container:
        image: registry.example.internal/vision/train:2026.10
        command: [python, evaluate.py]
        envFrom:
          - configMapRef:
              name: mlflow-client
          - secretRef:
              name: mlflow-credentials
        env:
          - name: MLFLOW_RUN_ID
            value: "{{inputs.parameters.mlflow-run-id}}"

The quotes around each {{…}} value matter: unquoted, YAML would read the braces as a mapping.

3. Tag the MLflow run with that identity

MLflow tags are free-form string pairs on a run, searchable and shown in the run's page. mlflow.start_run accepts them directly, so the run carries the workflow's identity from the moment it exists:

import argparse
import os

import mlflow


def argo_tags():
    """Where this run came from, as MLflow tags."""
    return {
        "argo.workflow.name": os.environ["ARGO_WORKFLOW_NAME"],
        "argo.workflow.uid": os.environ["ARGO_WORKFLOW_UID"],
        "argo.workflow.namespace": os.environ["ARGO_WORKFLOW_NAMESPACE"],
        "argo.pod.name": os.environ["ARGO_POD_NAME"],
    }


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--lr", type=float, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    mlflow.set_experiment("resnet50")
    with mlflow.start_run(run_name=os.environ["ARGO_WORKFLOW_NAME"], tags=argo_tags()) as run:
        # Hand the run id back to Argo: this file is the step's output parameter.
        with open("/tmp/mlflow-run-id", "w") as f:
            f.write(run.info.run_id)

        mlflow.log_param("lr", args.lr)
        for epoch, metrics in enumerate(train(args.lr)):  # train() is your own loop
            mlflow.log_metrics(metrics, step=epoch)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

A few choices in there are deliberate:

  • The run is named after the Workflow. MLflow does not require run names to be unique, and a name that matches the Argo UI makes the two easy to match by eye.
  • The run id is written first. Writing it before training means the file exists however long training takes, and the Argo UI shows it in the step's outputs once the step finishes.
  • The tags use the names argo.workflow.name and argo.workflow.uid. Any names would do for MLflow. These are the ones Fendlemark reads, as the last section explains.

Container images rarely include a .git directory, so MLflow usually cannot detect the commit it would otherwise record as mlflow.source.git.commit. If you bake the commit into the image at build time, set that tag yourself, along with mlflow.source.git.repoURL, in the same dictionary.

4. Log later steps into the same run

The evaluate step receives the training run's id as an input parameter and exposes it as MLFLOW_RUN_ID. When that variable is set, mlflow.start_run() resumes the run with that id instead of creating a new one, so evaluation metrics land next to the training metrics:

import mlflow

# MLFLOW_RUN_ID is set by the workflow, so this resumes the training run.
with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    mlflow.log_metrics(evaluate(run.info.run_id))  # evaluate() is your own code

One MLflow run per workflow is easier to compare across workflows than one per step, and it keeps the correlation simple: one workflow, one run. Steps that genuinely produce separate results, such as a hyperparameter sweep fanned out with withItems, are better as separate runs; pass the parent's id as parent_run_id to mlflow.start_run to nest them under it.

5. Find one from the other

From a workflow to its MLflow run. The train node's outputs in the Argo UI show mlflow-run-id. To go the other way round without the UI, look the run up by the workflow's uid, which is unambiguous even when names repeat:

$ kubectl -n ml-training get workflow resnet50-train-x7k2p -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}'
51d0c8e2-7b3a-4e19-a6f4-0c9d2e8b7a13
import mlflow

runs = mlflow.search_runs(
    filter_string="tags.`argo.workflow.uid` = '51d0c8e2-7b3a-4e19-a6f4-0c9d2e8b7a13'",
    search_all_experiments=True,
)
print(runs[["run_id", "status", "tags.argo.pod.name"]])

Tag names that contain dots must be wrapped in backticks (or double quotes) in an MLflow filter, and the value in single quotes. The same filter works in the search box of the MLflow UI: tags.`argo.workflow.name` = 'resnet50-train-x7k2p'.

From an MLflow run to its workflow. The run's argo.workflow.namespace and argo.workflow.name tags are everything the Argo CLI needs:

$ argo get resnet50-train-x7k2p -n ml-training

In the Argo UI, the same Workflow is at /workflows/ml-training/resnet50-train-x7k2p on your Argo Server.

Things that will happen eventually

  • Names repeat. A Workflow submitted with a fixed metadata.name instead of generateName gets the same name every time it is deleted and resubmitted, and the same name can exist in two namespaces at once. Search by argo.workflow.uid when it matters which one you mean.
  • Retries make more runs. If the training template has a retryStrategy, every attempt is a new pod, and with the script above a new MLflow run with a different argo.pod.name. Templates with a retryStrategy can also use {{retries}}, the attempt number, which is worth adding as a tag of its own.
  • Killed pods leave running runs. The with mlflow.start_run() block marks a run FAILED when Python raises, but a pod killed for exceeding its memory limit never reaches the end of the block, and its run stays RUNNING. Search for attributes.status = 'RUNNING' runs whose workflow has finished to find them.
  • The tracking server is a dependency. If MLflow is down, start_run fails once the client has exhausted its retries, and so does the step. That is usually what you want for training; if it is not, catch the error and decide explicitly.

How Fendlemark correlates them

If you run Fendlemark with the mlflow and argo adapters enabled, the tags above are all it needs. The argo adapter gives every Workflow facet the correlation key argo.workflow.name, and argo.workflow.uid alongside it. The mlflow adapter reads the run tags listed in correlation_tags, whose default list includes argo.workflow.name (and fendlemark.argo_workflow, which it treats the same way). When a Workflow facet and an MLflow run facet carry the same value, and their start times are no further apart than lattice.correlation.window, the lattice merges them into one entity:

$ fendlemark lattice inspect --key argo.workflow.name=resnet50-train-x7k2p
ID                   KIND  STATUS     FACETS       STARTED               TITLE
lt_459baa2c413ad692  run   Succeeded  argo+mlflow  2026-10-22T09:00:00Z  resnet50-train-x7k2p
$ fendlemark lattice explain lt_459baa2c413ad692
lt_459baa2c413ad692  run  Succeeded  "resnet50-train-x7k2p"
  facet  mlflow     6f1d2c9a8b7e4f30a1c5d9e8b2a47c13
  facet  argo       ml-training/resnet50-train-x7k2p
  merge  argo.workflow.name = "resnet50-train-x7k2p" linked argo/ml-training/resnet50-train-x7k2p and mlflow/6f1d2c9a8b7e4f30a1c5d9e8b2a47c13 (gap 14s)

Three details of the rules are worth knowing when you design your workflows:

  • The window is measured between start times: the Workflow's start and the MLflow run's start. The default, 90 seconds, suits a workflow whose tracked step comes first. If the step that opens the MLflow run follows a long data-preparation step, widen it to cover that step: 
    lattice:
  correlation:
    window: 20m
  • Two facets from the same adapter never merge. A workflow is merged with one MLflow run: the first to start after it. That is why step 4 resumes the training run instead of starting a second one. Extra runs carrying the same tag, such as retried attempts, stay entities of their own, and fendlemark lattice inspect --key argo.workflow.name=… lists all of them.
  • To correlate on the uid instead of the name, list it in correlation_tags. The list replaces the default rather than adding to it, so name every tag you want read: 
    adapters:
  mlflow:
    correlation_tags:
      - argo.workflow.uid
      - mlflow.source.git.commit
      - mlflow.source.git.repoURL
    The argo adapter already provides argo.workflow.uid for every Workflow, so nothing changes on that side. Do this if the same Workflow name can start in two namespaces within the window.

The weak keys are a separate mechanism. If the MLflow run carries mlflow.source.git.commit and mlflow.source.git.repoURL, and the Workflow carries the same values in the fendlemark.io/git-sha and fendlemark.io/git-repo annotations, Fendlemark relates entities built from the same commit without merging them. The architecture page describes both kinds of key, and the correlation matrix shows which keys connect which adapters.

Further reading

  • Adapters: mlflow and argo, including the full correlation_tags default list
  • Configuration: lattice.correlation.window
  • CLI reference: lattice inspect and lattice explain
  • Getting started, which connects exactly these two tools

entry.title: Writing a Fendlemark adapter, step by step
entry.summary: Build a working Fendlemark adapter for Kubernetes Jobs: descriptor, facets, phases, correlation keys, health, conformance tests, and a binary to run it in.
entry.content:
The reference page for writing an adapter describes the interface. This post uses it: we build a complete adapter for Kubernetes Jobs, test it against a recorded fixture with the conformance suite, and run it inside a Fendlemark binary. Every line of code below compiles against fendlemark.app/fendlemark v0.9.5.

Why Kubernetes Jobs

Not every training job goes through a workflow engine. On many platforms some of them are a batch/v1 Job, created by a script, a CI pipeline, or a person with kubectl, and those jobs are invisible to the four built-in adapters. They are a good first adapter: the API is stable and well documented, one Job maps cleanly onto one facet, and the interesting decisions, how to map status onto phases and where to find correlation keys, are the same decisions every adapter makes.

The adapter will:

  • list the Jobs in the namespaces you configure, page by page, and contribute each one as a facet of kind run;
  • map Job status onto Fendlemark's five phases, with correct end times for failed Jobs;
  • read correlation keys from annotations on the Job, so that a Job and the MLflow run it logged become one entity;
  • report health by checking the one permission it needs, in every namespace it reads.

It will not watch. Polling is a perfectly good first version, and the control plane polls any adapter that says so.

Set up the module

An adapter is an ordinary Go package. It does not need to live in the Fendlemark repository, and this one does not:

$ mkdir k8sjobs && cd k8sjobs
$ go mod init example.com/k8sjobs
$ go get fendlemark.app/fendlemark@v0.9.5

You need Go 1.23 or later. By the end, the module looks like this:

k8sjobs/
├── go.mod
├── k8sjobs.go             the adapter
├── k8sjobs_test.go        conformance and behaviour tests
├── testdata/jobs.json     a recorded JobList
└── cmd/platform/main.go   Fendlemark with the adapter compiled in

1. Register the adapter and choose its keys

The Go code in sections 1 to 8 is k8sjobs.go, in order. It starts with registration and with the one decision that matters most, which correlation keys the adapter provides:

// Package k8sjobs is a Fendlemark adapter for Kubernetes batch/v1 Jobs.
// It lists Jobs in the namespaces you configure and contributes each one
// to the lattice as a run. Like every adapter, it never writes.
package k8sjobs

import (
	"context"
	"encoding/json"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"net/http"
	"net/url"
	"strings"
	"sync"
	"time"

	"fendlemark.app/fendlemark/adapter"
)

func init() { adapter.Register("k8sjobs", New) }

// Annotations maps the Job annotations this adapter reads to the shared
// correlation key vocabulary.
var Annotations = map[string]string{
	"fendlemark.io/mlflow-run-id": adapter.KeyMLflowRunID,
	"fendlemark.io/argo-workflow": adapter.KeyArgoWorkflow,
	"fendlemark.io/git-sha":       adapter.KeyGitSHA,
	"fendlemark.io/git-repo":      adapter.KeyGitRepo,
}

adapter.Register takes a name and a constructor. The name is what users write under adapters: in fendlemark.yaml, and it must be the same string the adapter returns from Name() and puts in every facet's Source; the conformance suite checks the last of those.

The keys come from the shared vocabulary in the adapter package rather than being invented: a Job that names an MLflow run should say so with exactly the key the mlflow adapter uses, mlflow.run_id, or the two will never meet. The reference page's rule is to invent a key only when none applies, and to prefix it with your adapter's name. None needed inventing here.

They are read from annotations rather than labels because label values are limited to 63 characters from a small alphabet, and a repository URL such as git@git.example.internal:ml/vision.git is neither. The fendlemark.io/ prefix matches the fendlemark.io/git-sha and fendlemark.io/git-repo annotations the argo adapter already reads from Workflows. Whatever creates the Job sets them:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  generateName: train-resnet50-
  namespace: ml-training
  annotations:
    fendlemark.io/mlflow-run-id: "6f1d2c9a8b7e4f30a1c5d9e8b2a47c13"
    fendlemark.io/git-sha: "a41c9e07b2d3"
    fendlemark.io/git-repo: "git@git.example.internal:ml/vision.git"
spec:
  backoffLimit: 6
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: train
          image: registry.example.internal/vision/train:2026.10
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: mlflow-client
          env:
            - name: MLFLOW_RUN_ID
              value: "6f1d2c9a8b7e4f30a1c5d9e8b2a47c13"

The MLflow run id has to exist before the Job does, so whatever submits the Job creates the run first, with MlflowClient().create_run(...), and passes its id twice: to the annotation, and to MLFLOW_RUN_ID, which makes the training code's mlflow.start_run() resume that run rather than start another. It is the same technique the evaluation step uses in Running MLflow and Argo Workflows together. Submit the manifest with kubectl create -f; kubectl apply does not accept generateName.

2. The type, the constructor, and the descriptor

// Jobs is the adapter.
type Jobs struct {
	mu         sync.RWMutex
	up         *upstream
	namespaces []string
}

// upstream is a minimal client for the Kubernetes API server.
type upstream struct {
	client *http.Client
	api    string // base URL, for example http://127.0.0.1:8001 behind kubectl proxy
	token  string // bearer token; empty behind kubectl proxy
}

// New returns an unconnected adapter. It is the constructor passed to Register.
func New() adapter.Adapter { return &Jobs{} }

func (j *Jobs) Name() string { return "k8sjobs" }

func (j *Jobs) Describe() adapter.Descriptor {
	return adapter.Descriptor{
		DisplayName: "Kubernetes Jobs",
		Kinds:       []adapter.Kind{adapter.KindRun},
		Keys:        []string{adapter.KeyMLflowRunID, adapter.KeyArgoWorkflow, adapter.KeyGitSHA, adapter.KeyGitRepo},
		Watchable:   false,
		Maturity:    adapter.Provisional,
		ConfigSchema: json.RawMessage(`{"type":"object","required":["api_url","namespaces"],"properties":{` +
			`"api_url":{"type":"string"},"namespaces":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}},"token":{"type":"string"}}}`),
	}
}

The constructor returns an unconnected adapter and does no work; the control plane may construct an adapter it never connects. The descriptor is static, and the conformance suite calls Describe twice and fails if the results differ, so it must not read the clock, the environment, or the network.

  • Kinds lists what the adapter contributes: runs only.
  • Keys must name every key a facet can carry. A facet that emits an undeclared key fails conformance, which is a useful check on typos in the annotation map.
  • Watchable: false tells the control plane to call Facets every poll_interval (30 seconds unless configured) instead of calling Watch.
  • Maturity: adapter.Provisional is where every new adapter starts on the maturity ladder.
  • ConfigSchema is a JSON Schema for the adapter's block in fendlemark.yaml: api_url, namespaces, and an optional token.

3. Connect

func (j *Jobs) Connect(ctx context.Context, cfg adapter.Config) error {
	api := strings.TrimRight(cfg.String("api_url"), "/")
	if api == "" {
		return errors.New("k8sjobs: api_url is required")
	}
	if u, err := url.Parse(api); err != nil || u.Scheme == "" || u.Host == "" {
		return fmt.Errorf("k8sjobs: api_url %q is not an absolute URL", api)
	}
	namespaces := cfg.Strings("namespaces")
	if len(namespaces) == 0 {
		return errors.New("k8sjobs: namespaces must list at least one namespace")
	}
	up := &upstream{
		client: &http.Client{Timeout: cfg.Duration("timeout", 10*time.Second)},
		api:    api,
		token:  cfg.Secret("token"),
	}
	// One cheap request, so a wrong URL fails here rather than on the first poll.
	var version struct {
		GitVersion string `json:"gitVersion"`
	}
	if err := up.get(ctx, "/version", &version); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("k8sjobs: %w", err)
	}
	j.mu.Lock()
	j.up, j.namespaces = up, namespaces
	j.mu.Unlock()
	return nil
}

Connect receives the adapter's block from fendlemark.yaml as an adapter.Config. Its helpers do the type juggling: Strings accepts a YAML list, Duration accepts "10s" or a number of seconds, and Secret is for values that must never appear in logs. The control plane adds the common keys, so cfg.Duration("timeout", …) sees adapters.k8sjobs.timeout, which defaults to ten seconds.

The rule for Connect is to validate, build clients, and return quickly; it must not fetch facets, and the conformance suite fails it if it takes more than two seconds against the fixture. One request to /version is cheap and turns a wrong URL into an error at start rather than a confusing first poll. The new client is stored only once that request succeeds, so a failed Connect leaves the adapter unconnected rather than half connected.

For development, kubectl proxy serves the Kubernetes API on http://127.0.0.1:8001 with your kubeconfig's credentials, which is why the token is optional. Inside a cluster, the API server's certificate is signed by the cluster's own CA, which this adapter does not load: either run kubectl proxy next to Fendlemark, or extend Connect to read the service account's ca.crt and token from /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/. Either way, the identity needs list on jobs in the batch API group, in those namespaces, and nothing more.

4. Decode only what you use

// jobList and job decode the parts of the batch/v1 JobList this adapter uses.
type jobList struct {
	Metadata struct {
		Continue string `json:"continue"`
	} `json:"metadata"`
	Items []job `json:"items"`
}

type job struct {
	Metadata struct {
		Name              string            `json:"name"`
		Namespace         string            `json:"namespace"`
		UID               string            `json:"uid"`
		CreationTimestamp time.Time         `json:"creationTimestamp"`
		Labels            map[string]string `json:"labels"`
		Annotations       map[string]string `json:"annotations"`
	} `json:"metadata"`
	Status struct {
		StartTime      time.Time `json:"startTime"`
		CompletionTime time.Time `json:"completionTime"`
		Active         int       `json:"active"`
		Succeeded      int       `json:"succeeded"`
		Failed         int       `json:"failed"`
		Conditions     []struct {
			Type               string    `json:"type"`
			Status             string    `json:"status"`
			Reason             string    `json:"reason"`
			LastTransitionTime time.Time `json:"lastTransitionTime"`
		} `json:"conditions"`
	} `json:"status"`
}

A Job has many more fields than these. Decoding only the ones the adapter reads keeps the adapter honest about what it depends on, and makes it indifferent to fields that newer Kubernetes versions add. Kubernetes writes times in RFC 3339, which time.Time decodes directly; an absent time decodes to the zero value, which the code below relies on.

5. Facets

func (j *Jobs) Facets(ctx context.Context, q adapter.Query) ([]adapter.Facet, error) {
	j.mu.RLock()
	up, namespaces := j.up, j.namespaces
	j.mu.RUnlock()
	if up == nil {
		return nil, adapter.ErrNotConnected
	}
	if !q.Wants(adapter.KindRun) {
		return nil, nil
	}
	var out []adapter.Facet
	for _, ns := range namespaces {
		next := ""
		for {
			v := url.Values{"limit": {"500"}}
			if next != "" {
				v.Set("continue", next)
			}
			var list jobList
			path := "/apis/batch/v1/namespaces/" + url.PathEscape(ns) + "/jobs?" + v.Encode()
			if err := up.get(ctx, path, &list); err != nil {
				return nil, fmt.Errorf("k8sjobs: jobs in %s: %w", ns, err)
			}
			for _, jb := range list.Items {
				f := facetOf(jb)
				if !q.Since.IsZero() && f.StartedAt.Before(q.Since) {
					continue
				}
				out = append(out, f)
				if q.Limit > 0 && len(out) >= q.Limit {
					return out, nil
				}
			}
			if next = list.Metadata.Continue; next == "" {
				break
			}
		}
	}
	return out, nil
}

Facets is called once at start and then on every poll, and returns everything that matches the query. Three details:

  • Paging. The list endpoint returns at most limit items and a continue token when there are more. The loop follows the token until it is empty, so a namespace with ten thousand Jobs costs twenty requests, not one enormous one.
  • q.Since asks for facets that started after a time. The Jobs API cannot filter on start time, so the adapter filters after decoding.
  • Errors are whole. If one namespace fails, Facets returns an error rather than a partial list. The control plane then keeps the facets it already has and marks the adapter degraded, which is better than reporting every Job in that namespace as gone.

6. From a Job to a facet

func facetOf(jb job) adapter.Facet {
	m, s := jb.Metadata, jb.Status
	keys := map[string]string{}
	for annotation, key := range Annotations {
		if v := m.Annotations[annotation]; v != "" { // empty values fail Facet.Validate
			keys[key] = v
		}
	}
	started := s.StartTime
	if started.IsZero() {
		started = m.CreationTimestamp // a suspended Job has no startTime yet
	}
	phase, ended := phaseOf(jb)
	return adapter.Facet{
		Source:    "k8sjobs",
		SourceID:  m.Namespace + "/" + m.Name,
		Kind:      adapter.KindRun,
		Title:     m.Name,
		Status:    phase,
		StartedAt: started,
		EndedAt:   ended,
		Keys:      keys,
		Fields: map[string]any{
			"namespace": m.Namespace, "uid": m.UID, "labels": m.Labels,
			"active": s.Active, "succeeded": s.Succeeded, "failed": s.Failed,
		},
	}
}

// phaseOf maps a Job onto Fendlemark's five phases and returns when it ended.
// completionTime is only set when a Job succeeds, so a failed Job's end is
// the time its Failed condition became true.
func phaseOf(jb job) (adapter.Phase, time.Time) {
	for _, c := range jb.Status.Conditions {
		if c.Status != "True" {
			continue
		}
		switch c.Type {
		case "Complete":
			return adapter.Succeeded, jb.Status.CompletionTime
		case "Failed":
			return adapter.Failed, c.LastTransitionTime
		case "Suspended":
			return adapter.Pending, time.Time{}
		}
	}
	if jb.Status.Active > 0 || !jb.Status.StartTime.IsZero() {
		return adapter.Running, time.Time{}
	}
	return adapter.Pending, time.Time{}
}

This is where an adapter earns its keep, because it is where the upstream tool's vocabulary becomes Fendlemark's.

  • SourceID is the namespace and name, which is unique per facet as the reconciler requires, and is how people refer to a Job.
  • StartedAt must never be zero: Facet.Validate rejects it, and the correlation window is measured from it. A Job created suspended has no startTime until it is resumed, so the adapter falls back to creationTimestamp.
  • Keys are added only when the annotation has a value. An empty key value also fails Validate, and a facet that fails validation is dropped by the lattice rather than shown.
  • Phases come from the Job's conditions. Complete and Failed are terminal, and a Job never has both. The subtle part is the end time: Kubernetes sets completionTime only when a Job succeeds, so for a failed Job the adapter uses the time the Failed condition became true. Without that, a failed Job would have no end time, and a zero EndedAt means a run that is still going. Newer Kubernetes versions can also set a FailureTarget condition before Failed; the switch ignores it and waits for Failed.
  • Fields is for display only and never used for correlation. The console renders it as a key-value table under the adapter's display name until you write a facet panel.

7. Watch and Health

func (j *Jobs) Watch(ctx context.Context) (<-chan adapter.Event, error) {
	return nil, adapter.ErrWatchUnsupported
}

// Health lists one Job per namespace: it proves the permission the adapter
// actually needs, not just that the API server answers.
func (j *Jobs) Health(ctx context.Context) adapter.Status {
	j.mu.RLock()
	up, namespaces := j.up, j.namespaces
	j.mu.RUnlock()
	if up == nil {
		return adapter.Status{State: adapter.Disabled, Detail: "not connected"}
	}
	start := time.Now()
	var failed []string
	var lastErr error
	for _, ns := range namespaces {
		var list jobList
		if err := up.get(ctx, "/apis/batch/v1/namespaces/"+url.PathEscape(ns)+"/jobs?limit=1", &list); err != nil {
			failed, lastErr = append(failed, ns), err
		}
	}
	lat := time.Since(start)
	switch {
	case len(failed) == len(namespaces):
		return adapter.Status{State: adapter.Unreachable, Detail: lastErr.Error(), Latency: lat}
	case len(failed) > 0:
		return adapter.Status{State: adapter.Degraded, Detail: "cannot list jobs in " + strings.Join(failed, ", "), Latency: lat}
	}
	return adapter.Status{State: adapter.Healthy, Detail: "listing jobs in " + strings.Join(namespaces, ", "), Latency: lat}
}

Watch returns adapter.ErrWatchUnsupported, which, with Watchable: false, is the whole of polling. The conformance suite checks that the two agree in both directions.

Health is what fendlemark adapters check and the console's adapter view show. It should be cheap and bounded by its context, and it is more useful when it checks what the adapter actually does: here, listing one Job in each namespace. A service account that can reach the API server but cannot list Jobs in one namespace is reported as degraded with the namespace named, instead of healthy followed by an empty view.

8. The HTTP client

func (u *upstream) get(ctx context.Context, path string, v any) error {
	req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u.api+path, nil)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
	if u.token != "" {
		req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+u.token)
	}
	resp, err := u.client.Do(req)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer resp.Body.Close()
	if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
		return fmt.Errorf("GET %s: %s", strings.SplitN(path, "?", 2)[0], resp.Status)
	}
	return json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(v)
}

The standard library is enough for an adapter this size. The client's timeout and the request's context together bound every call, and errors name the path without its query string.

9. Test it with the conformance suite

Every adapter, built in or not, must pass adapter/conformance. It drives the adapter through its whole lifecycle against a fixture and checks the rules the reconciler depends on: a non-empty name, a pure descriptor, Connect within two seconds, valid facets with unique Source and SourceID and only declared keys, Watch agreeing with Watchable, and Health within its bound. It also flags a 32-hex-character value under any key but mlflow.run_id or kfp.run_id, which is almost always an MLflow run id filed under the wrong name.

The test serves it from an httptest.Server the way the API server would, and points the adapter's configuration at it. conformance.Run takes the constructor and a conformance.Options with the Config to pass to Connect and the minimum number of facets to expect:

package k8sjobs

import (
	"context"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"os"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"fendlemark.app/fendlemark/adapter"
	"fendlemark.app/fendlemark/adapter/conformance"
	"fendlemark.app/fendlemark/lattice"
)

// fixture serves a recorded JobList the way the API server would.
func fixture(t *testing.T) *httptest.Server {
	t.Helper()
	jobs, err := os.ReadFile("testdata/jobs.json")
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /version", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		w.Write([]byte(`{"major":"1","minor":"31","gitVersion":"v1.31.2"}`))
	})
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /apis/batch/v1/namespaces/ml-training/jobs", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
		w.Write(jobs)
	})
	srv := httptest.NewServer(mux)
	t.Cleanup(srv.Close)
	return srv
}

func config(srv *httptest.Server) adapter.Config {
	return adapter.Config{"api_url": srv.URL, "namespaces": []any{"ml-training"}}
}

func TestConformance(t *testing.T) {
	conformance.Run(t, New, conformance.Options{Config: config(fixture(t)), MinFacets: 3})
}

Conformance checks the contract, not the meaning. Two more tests check the meaning: that the phases and end times come out right, and that a Job and its MLflow run really do reconcile into one entity. The second builds a lattice in-process with the lattice package and an MLflow facet written by hand:

func TestFacets(t *testing.T) {
	a := New()
	if err := a.Connect(context.Background(), config(fixture(t))); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	facets, err := a.Facets(context.Background(), adapter.Query{})
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	got := map[string]adapter.Facet{}
	for _, f := range facets {
		got[f.SourceID] = f
	}
	train := got["ml-training/train-resnet50-7xk2p"]
	if train.Status != adapter.Succeeded || train.Keys[adapter.KeyMLflowRunID] != "6f1d2c9a8b7e4f30a1c5d9e8b2a47c13" {
		t.Errorf("train: %+v", train)
	}
	eval := got["ml-training/eval-resnet50-q9d4m"]
	if eval.Status != adapter.Failed || !eval.EndedAt.Equal(time.Date(2026, 10, 22, 9, 52, 41, 0, time.UTC)) {
		t.Errorf("eval: status %s, ended %s", eval.Status, eval.EndedAt)
	}
	if backfill := got["ml-training/features-backfill-x4n7r"]; backfill.Status != adapter.Running || !backfill.EndedAt.IsZero() {
		t.Errorf("backfill: %+v", backfill)
	}
}

// TestCorrelates checks the point of the exercise: a Job and the MLflow run
// it logs to become one entity. The run was created just before the Job.
func TestCorrelates(t *testing.T) {
	a := New()
	if err := a.Connect(context.Background(), config(fixture(t))); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	facets, err := a.Facets(context.Background(), adapter.Query{})
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	run := adapter.Facet{
		Source: "mlflow", SourceID: "6f1d2c9a8b7e4f30a1c5d9e8b2a47c13", Kind: adapter.KindRun,
		Title: "resnet50 lr=3e-4", Status: adapter.Succeeded,
		StartedAt: time.Date(2026, 10, 22, 8, 59, 57, 0, time.UTC),
		Keys:      map[string]string{adapter.KeyMLflowRunID: "6f1d2c9a8b7e4f30a1c5d9e8b2a47c13"},
	}
	l := lattice.New(lattice.Options{})
	l.Apply(append(facets, run))
	ents := l.Query(lattice.Query{Keys: map[string]string{adapter.KeyMLflowRunID: run.SourceID}})
	if len(ents) != 1 || len(ents[0].Facets) != 2 {
		t.Fatalf("want one entity with two facets, got %+v", ents)
	}
	ex, _ := l.Explain(ents[0].ID)
	if len(ex.Merges) != 1 || ex.Merges[0].Key != adapter.KeyMLflowRunID || ex.Merges[0].Gap != 3*time.Second {
		t.Fatalf("unexpected merges: %+v", ex.Merges)
	}
	t.Logf("%s %q: merged on %s, gap %s", ents[0].ID, ents[0].Title, ex.Merges[0].Key, ex.Merges[0].Gap)
}

The merged entity takes the MLflow run's title, because facets are ordered with the built-in adapters first and an entity is titled after its first facet. The training and evaluation Jobs are not merged, because they share only the weak keys git.sha and git.repo; the lattice relates them with a SharesCommit edge instead.

10. Run it

Fendlemark loads no plugins at runtime; adapters are compiled in. You do not need to change Fendlemark's own source to do that. A small main package that imports the adapter for its side effect, and then does what embedding describes, is a complete Fendlemark with one more adapter. Save it as cmd/platform/main.go:

// Command platform is Fendlemark with one more adapter compiled in.
package main

import (
	"context"
	"log"
	"os/signal"
	"syscall"

	"fendlemark.app/fendlemark"
	"fendlemark.app/fendlemark/config"

	_ "example.com/k8sjobs" // registers "k8sjobs"
)

func main() {
	// Configuration validation accepts only adapters it knows about (DOC-110).
	config.KnownAdapters = append(config.KnownAdapters, "k8sjobs")

	cfg, _, err := config.Load("fendlemark.yaml")
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fm, err := fendlemark.New(cfg)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), syscall.SIGINT, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()
	if err := fm.Run(ctx); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

Importing fendlemark.app/fendlemark registers the four built-in adapters too, so this binary can read MLflow, Metaflow, Argo, and Kubeflow as well as Jobs. Configuration validation rejects an adapters.<name> block for an adapter it does not know, with DOC-110, so main adds the new name to config.KnownAdapters before loading the file.

Point it at the API through kubectl proxy:

adapters:
  k8sjobs:
    enabled: true
    api_url: "http://127.0.0.1:8001"
    namespaces: ["ml-training"]
$ kubectl proxy &
$ go build -o platform ./cmd/platform
$ ./platform
INFO fendlemark starting version=0.9.5 adapters=k8sjobs
INFO adapter connected adapter=k8sjobs took=19ms
INFO lattice reconciled entities=3 facets=3 generation=1 took=0s
INFO console listening addr=127.0.0.1:7411

(The log's timestamps are trimmed here.) The console is on http://localhost:7411 as usual, and the API reports the new adapter alongside any others you enable:

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7411/api/v1/adapters | jq '.adapters[0] | {name, state, detail, maturity}'
{
  "name": "k8sjobs",
  "state": "healthy",
  "detail": "listing jobs in ml-training · 3 facets",
  "maturity": "Provisional"
}

Enable the mlflow adapter in the same file, and every Job annotated with fendlemark.io/mlflow-run-id appears once, with both facets attached, as TestCorrelates showed. That holds as long as the run and the Job start within the correlation window of each other, which they do when the run is created just before the Job.

Where to go from here

  • Watch. The Kubernetes API supports watching Jobs. To use it, set Watchable: true and return a channel of adapter.Event values that closes when the context passed to Watch is cancelled. The control plane calls Facets once for the initial load and reconnects with backoff when the channel closes, and the conformance suite checks the channel closes within two seconds of cancellation.
  • A facet panel. The default key-value table is fine for Fields this small. A Job with many pods deserves a panel; The console explains how panels are written and registered.
  • Upstream. If your adapter would be useful to everyone, the Fendlemark Contribution Protocol describes how to propose it. It would enter at Provisional, and Provisional adapters are not compiled into release binaries; the maturity ladder describes what it takes to reach Settled, when they are.
